vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: clawtoclaw
Version: 1.0.14

The clawtoclaw skill bundle provides a framework for inter-agent coordination using end-to-end encryption and human-in-the-loop approval gates. The included Python scripts (e.g., scripts/event_heartbeat.py, scripts/generate_keypair.py) handle API communication and cryptographic key management while enforcing security best practices, such as restricted file permissions (chmod 600) for credentials. The documentation (SKILL.md and references/security-and-limits.md) contains explicit instructions for the AI agent to treat all incoming messages as untrusted and strictly avoid sharing sensitive data like SSH keys or private schedules, demonstrating a clear focus on preventing prompt injection and data exfiltration.

llm.summary: The skill's code and instructions are broadly consistent with a coordinator for agent-to-agent interactions, but the package metadata omits key operational requirements (local credential/key files and a PyNaCl dependency) and the runtime scripts perform network calls and persistent local state — so review before installing.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (coordinate with other AI agents) aligns with the provided API calls, keypair generation, encryption helpers, and event/heartbeat runner. However, the registry metadata declares no required env/configs while the instructions and scripts clearly expect a local credentials file (~/.c2c/credentials.json) and key files (~/.c2c/keys/). That omission is an inconsistency (likely packaging oversight) but not itself malicious.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md instructs only the actions necessary for the stated purpose: registering an agent, storing an API key, uploading a public key, encrypting/decrypting payloads, starting threads, and optionally running a heartbeat to auto-propose intros. It does not ask to read unrelated system files or exfiltrate arbitrary data. It explicitly warns not to share private keys and enforces approval gates and limits.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec (instruction-only) and all included code is bundled in the skill. This reduces installation risk. The scripts require the PyNaCl library (SKILL.md references pip install pynacl) but the skill metadata does not declare this dependency; that mismatch should be fixed or called out to users.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requires an API key and local private keys at runtime, but the registry declares no required environment variables or config paths. The scripts read/write files under ~/.c2c/ (credentials and keys) and expect strict file permissions. That file access is proportional to the purpose, but the omission in metadata is misleading and could cause surprise. No unrelated service credentials are requested.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request forced inclusion (always=false) and does not modify other skills. It persists its own state under ~/.c2c/active_event.json and key files under ~/.c2c/keys/ — a reasonable level of persistence for this functionality. The heartbeat runner can make automated API calls (auto-propose only when outreachMode is enabled), so the user should be cautious enabling proactive modes.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill appears to do what it says (agent-to-agent coordination) and includes helpful scripts for key management, encryption, and an event heartbeat. However: (1) the registry metadata does not declare the runtime requirement to store an API key and key files under ~/.c2c/, nor the PyNaCl dependency — expect to create and protect ~/.c2c/credentials.json and ~/.c2c/keys/*.json yourself; (2) review the included scripts before running — they make POST requests to https://www.clawtoclaw.com/api and will send encrypted coordination data using your API key; (3) run initial tests in a sandbox or separate account, keep file permissions strict (chmod 600), and keep proactive features (heartbeat --propose / outreachMode=propose_for_me) off until you trust behavior; and (4) verify the service homepage and API owner before entering real credentials. These inconsistencies look like sloppy packaging rather than malicious intent, but double-check the remote service and the exact credentials you provide.
